[[File:Eucalyptus saligna.JPG|thumb|''Eucalyptus saligna'' with rough lower trunk bark]]
'''''Eucalyptus saligna''''', commonly known as the '''Sydney blue gum''' or '''blue gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus saligna'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_saligna.htm|publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=29 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of medium-sized to tall tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Australia. It has rough, flaky bark near the base of the trunk, smooth bark above, lance-shaped to curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of seven, nine or eleven, white flowers and cylindrical to conical or cup-shaped fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus saligna'' is a tree with a straight trunk that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|30-55|m}}, rarely to {{cvt|65|m}}, a [[Diameter at breast height|dbh]] of {{cvt|2-2.5|m}}, and forms a [[lignotuber]]. The trunk has smooth pale grey or white bark with {{cvt|1-4|m}} of rough brownish bark at the base. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have lance-shaped to egg-shaped or oblong leaves that are paler on the lower surface, {{cvt|37-120|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-40|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, glossy green, paler on the lower surface, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|90-190|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-40|mm}} wide, on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|15-30|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of seven, nine or eleven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|5-15|mm}} long, the individual buds [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|5|mm}} long. Mature buds are spindle-shaped, oval or diamond-shaped, {{cvt|5-10|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical or beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from December to March and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cylindrical, conical or cup-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|4-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-7|mm}} wide with the valves protruding above the rim.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="floransw">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus saligna'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~saligna |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=18 December 2019}}</ref><ref name=Ben98/><ref name="Boland"/><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus saligna'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20saligna |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=18 December 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus saligna'' was first formally described in 1797 by English naturalist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in ''[[Linnean Society of London#Publications|Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]'', and still bears its original name.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus saligna''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455064|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="Sm.">{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=James Edward |title=Botanical Characters of Some Plants of the natural Order of Myrti |journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London |date=1797 |volume=3 |pages=285–286 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13713#page/312/mode/1up |access-date=18 December 2019}}</ref> The species name ''saligna'' refers to some likeness to a [[willow]], though what attribute this is, is unclear.<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|page=84|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CRQg11hSJ1kC&q=Eucalyptus+saligna+boland&pg=PA84}} Retrieved 12-24-2011.</ref> It has been classified in the subgenus ''Symphyomyrtus'', Section ''Latoangulatae'', Series ''Transversae'' (eastern blue gums) by [[Ian Brooker]] and [[David Kleinig]]. Its two closest relatives are the flooded gum (''[[Eucalyptus grandis|E. grandis]]'') and the mountain blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus deanei|E. deanei]]'').<ref name=brooker>{{cite book|title=Field Guide to Eucalypts|volume=1: South-eastern Australia|author1=Brooker, M.I.H. |author2=Kleinig, D. A. |pages=69–72 |publisher= Bloomings Books|location= Melbourne |year= 1999|isbn=1-876473-03-7}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Sydney blue gum is generally found within {{cvt|120|km|mi}} of the coastline in its range from [[Sydney]] to Maryborough in central Queensland. To the northwest, it is found in disjunct populations in central Queensland, including in [[Eungella National Park]], [[Kroombit Tops National Park|Kroombit Tops]], Consuelo Tableland, [[Blackdown Tableland National Park|Blackdown Tableland]] and [[Carnarvon Gorge]].<ref name="Boland"/> It grows in tall forests in more sheltered areas, on clay or loam soils, and alluvial sands.<ref name="Boland"/><ref name=Ben98/> It is a component of the endangered [[blue gum high forest]] ecological community in the Sydney region.<ref name=Ben98/> Populations found south of Sydney are now not considered to be ''E. saligna''.<ref name="floransw"/>

Associated trees include blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis|E. pilularis]]''), grey ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus paniculata|E. paniculata]]''), mountain blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus deanei|E. deanei]]''), flooded gum (''E. grandis''), tallowwood (''[[Eucalyptus microcorys|E. microcorys]]''), thin-leaved stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus eugenioides|E. eugenioides]]''), manna gum (''[[Eucalyptus viminalis|E. viminalis]]''), river peppermint (''[[Eucalyptus elata|E. elata]]''), grey gums (''[[Eucalyptus punctata|E. punctata]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus propinqua|E. propinqua]]'' ), rough-barked apple (''[[Angophora floribunda]]''), spotted gum (''[[Corymbia maculata]]''), turpentine (''[[Syncarpia glomulifera]]''), brush box (''[[Lophostemon confertus]]'') and forest oak (''[[Allocasuarina torulosa]]'').<ref name="Boland"/><ref name=Ben98/>

South of [[Port Jackson|Sydney Harbour]] and the [[Parramatta River]], pure stands of ''E. saligna'' give way to hybrid populations with bangalay (''[[Eucalyptus botryoides|E. botryoides]]'').<ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal |last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998 |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |page=926 |url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/045f8bca-7669-4777-bdac-9c18d855dc61/Volume-5(4)-1998-Cun5Ben808-987.pdf.aspx |access-date=2019-12-18 |archive-date=2022-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220202153352/https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/045f8bca-7669-4777-bdac-9c18d855dc61/Volume-5(4)-1998-Cun5Ben808-987.pdf.aspx }}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Eucalyptus saligna'' regenerates by regrowing from [[epicormic bud]]s on the trunk and lower branches after bushfire. Trees live for over two hundred years. The [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus'') eats the flowers, the [[koala]] (''Phascalarctos cinereus'') eats the leaves, and [[crimson rosella]] (''Platycercus elegans'') eats the seed.<ref name=Ben98/> The [[longhorn beetle]] species ''[[Paroplites australis]]'',<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hawkeswood |first=Trevor J. |year=1992 |title=Review of the biology, host plants and immature stages of the Australian Cerambycidae (Coleoptera). Part 1, Parandrinae and Prioninae |journal=Giornale Italiano di Entomologia |volume=6 |pages=207–224 |url=http://www.cerambycoidea.com/titles/hawskeswood160.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229112927/http://www.cerambycoidea.com/titles/hawskeswood160.pdf |archive-date=2010-12-29}}</ref> ''[[Agrianome spinicollis]]'' and ''[[Tessaromma undatum]]'' have been recorded from the Sydney blue gum.<ref name=Ben98/>

The presence of the territorial and aggressive [[bell miner]] (''Manorina melanophrys'') and psyllid insects (''[[Glycaspis]]'')  is correlated with dieback of the canopy of ''E. saligna'', a syndrome which has been termed bell-miner-associated dieback (BMAD), though the exact mechanism remains unclear.<ref name="bmad">{{cite journal|author1=Grant Wardell-Johnson|author2=Christine Stone|author3=Harry Recher|author4=A. Jasmyn J. Lynch|year=2005|title=Eucalypt dieback associated with bell miner habitat in south-eastern Australia|journal=Australian Forestry|volume=68|issue=4|pages=231–36|url=http://www.forestry.org.au/pdf/pdf-members/afj/AFJ%202005%20v68/AFJ%20December%202005%2068-4/W-Johnsonetal.pdf|doi=10.1080/00049158.2005.10674970|hdl=20.500.11937/43260|s2cid=62827173|access-date=2011-12-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321230656/http://www.forestry.org.au/pdf/pdf-members/afj/AFJ%202005%20v68/AFJ%20December%202005%2068-4/W-Johnsonetal.pdf|archive-date=2012-03-21|hdl-access=free}} Retrieved 12-24-2011.</ref> After colonization by ''[[Glycaspis]]'', ''E. salinga'' may then be infested by the [[ambrosia beetle]] ''[[Amasa truncata]]''.<ref name="GerholdMcdermott2013">{{cite book|author1=H. D. Gerhold|author2=R. E. Mcdermott|author3=E. J. Schreiner|title=Breeding Pest-Resistant Trees: Proceedings of a N.A.T.O. and N.S.F.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wq3YBAAAQBAJ|date=24 September 2013|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=978-1-4831-5838-9}}</ref>

==Uses==
The wood of this species is heavy (about {{cvt|850|kg/m3}}), fairly hard, coarse, even textured
and reasonably easy to work. It is used for general building construction, panelling, and boatbuilding, and is highly prized for flooring and furniture because of its rich dark honey colour.<ref>{{cite book|author=Bootle KR. |year=1983|title=Wood in Australia. Types, properties and uses|publisher= McGraw-Hill Book Company |location= Sydney|isbn=0-07-451047-9}}</ref>
